title: Heritage demolitions approved for supportive housing project
subtitle: Council also set a Bill 5 position, approved a Fairway Road North apartment, and ordered a dog designation review.
overview: Council approved heritage permits to demolish two houses at 11 Roy Street and 68 Queen Street North in the Civic Centre heritage district, going against the staff recommendation to refuse. The site is planned for affordable and supportive housing for adults with developmental disabilities. Demolition is conditional on a documentation and salvage plan, a commemoration plan, a building permit application and a registered development agreement. The vote was unanimous {{vote:m2}}.

On Bill 5, council defeated a motion to oppose the provincial special economic zone provisions {{vote:m5}}. It then backed an alternate motion supporting the Association of Municipalities of Ontario's position, which was unanimous {{vote:m4}}. Council also approved a multiple dwelling at 132 Fairway Road North, directed staff to report on dog designation follow-up by September 29, and asked the province to let municipalities charge fees for paper billing {{vote:m26}}.

Council also set a parkland acquisition strategy for early 2026, moved Idlewood Greenway funding forward and approved a property tax exemption for affordable housing on Lancaster Street West. Separately, the Mayor noted the September 6 deadline to request a small garbage bin from the Region of Waterloo. Staff were also asked to review dropping return envelopes from tax and utility bills.

decisions.item: Heritage permits, 11 Roy St and 68 Queen St N
decisions.detail: Council approved demolition of both houses for a supportive housing project, subject to salvage, commemoration, building permit and development agreement conditions.
Council approved the Official Plan and zoning changes allowing a multiple dwelling at a floor space ratio of 1.33, and endorsed the revised urban design brief.

Council supported the Association of Municipalities of Ontario's position, asking the province to require host municipality support for special economic zones and to protect species at risk and consult Indigenous communities.
Staff must report back by September 29, 2025 on notifying councillors of dangerous dog orders, periodic compliance reports and legislative changes for holding seized dogs.
Council asked the province to amend the Municipal Act so paper billing need not be the default and municipalities can charge fees for new paper-billing accounts.
Staff will develop a parkland acquisition strategy by March 31, 2026 and identify government-owned properties in each ward that could address parkland shortages.
Council moved $5.36M of 2026 funding from the Middle Strasburg Naturalization project to Idlewood Greenway and pre-approved it for tender in 2025.
Council approved a city property tax exemption for qualifying affordable housing units at 475-477 Lancaster Street West.

debate: On the heritage permits, delegates supporting the project described a shortage of supportive housing for adults with developmental disabilities. They said keeping the buildings was too costly and that the project would not proceed without demolition. Several councillors said housing need outweighed heritage loss in this case.

Heritage advocates and the staff recommendation argued that demolition is the most irreversible change in a heritage district. One delegate said the Queen Street house, a top-ranked heritage building, should be kept or integrated into the new building. Staff said council has legal authority to weigh broader public interests and suggested conditions and commemoration to protect against demolition without redevelopment.

On Bill 5, delegates urged council to oppose the special economic zone provisions, citing risks to municipal authority, environmental protections and Indigenous consultation. The mover said the province had shown no interest in collaborating. Other councillors preferred a motion mirroring the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, arguing a united municipal voice is more effective and less adversarial.

On paper billing, one councillor opposed fees for paper bills, saying they could burden people on fixed incomes or without reliable internet, and suggested incentives for e-billing instead. The mover said existing accounts would be grandfathered and that the paper billing cost is large.

On dog designations, councillors who sit on the appeal committee said there is no follow-up on whether designated dogs are surrendered or complying. They called the motion overdue to close that gap and to keep residents informed.
